@graph.text: Variation in inherited genetic or observable traits within or among offspring in a population.
Environmental conditions cause differential survival and reproduction associated with heritable trait variation, changing trait distributions over generations.
Heritable population characteristics change over time in relation to environmental conditions.
Fossils provide evidence for changes in organisms and life forms over time.

Understands the mechanisms of change (e.g., mutation and natural selection) that lead to adaptations in a species and their ability to survive naturally in changing conditions and to increase species diversity.

Understands how genetic variation of offspring contributes to population control in an environment and that natural selection ensures that those who are best adapted to their surroundings survive to reproduce.
Knows that the fossil record provides evidence that changes in the kinds of plants and animals in the environment have been occurring over time.
The same fossil-record benchmark is retained; the GLE places its specific expectation at eighth grade.

Explore the scientific theory of evolution by recognizing and explaining ways in which genetic variation and environmental factors contribute to evolution by natural selection and diversity of organisms.
Describe the conditions required for natural selection, including overproduction of offspring, inherited variation, and the struggle to survive, resulting in differential reproductive success.
Recognize the requirements for natural selection to occur in a population.

@graph.text: Climate patterns emerge from radiation balance, greenhouse processes, atmospheric and ocean circulation, and feedbacks.
Human activities interact with atmospheric, hydrologic, geologic, and biological Earth systems.
Natural and human influences, including Earth-system and astronomical conditions, contribute to changes in climate.
Cite evidence that the ocean has had a significant influence on climate change by absorbing, storing, and moving heat, carbon, and water.
Identify, analyze, and relate the internal (Earth system) and external (astronomical) conditions that contribute to global climate change.
Knows that changes in Earth's climate, geological activity, and life forms may be traced and compared.
Knows that humans burn fossil fuels to release the stored energy as heat and carbon dioxide.
Analyze how population size is determined by births, deaths, immigration, emigration, and limiting factors (biotic and abiotic) that determine carrying capacity.
Explain how populations change over time as a result of births, deaths, immigration, emigration, and limiting factors.
@graph.crosswalkNote: The 2008 benchmark explicitly names births, deaths, immigration, emigration, and limiting factors as determinants of population size. Concept-level continuity only; no evidence of drafting access or borrowing.

@graph.text: Evaluate strategies related to sustainability and resilience using Earth system evidence.
@graph.crosswalkNote: Partial concept match with a change in decision context. Florida 2008 SC.912.L.17.13 calls for monitoring environmental parameters when making policy decisions (sources/2008/florida-2008-science-standards.txt:3600). The draft evaluates sustainability/resilience strategies using physical measurements, ecological indicators, population trends, and evidence of system response (sources/2026/fl-912.txt:7213–7237). It carries forward monitoring/evidence to evaluate environmental strategies, but does not explicitly frame that evidence as informing policy decisions. The draft adds resilience, trade-offs, limitations, and uncertainty. Concept continuity does not establish borrowing.

@graph.text: Model particle motion in solids, liquids, and gases.

@graph.text: Measure and compare properties of matter.
@graph.crosswalkNote: High-confidence concept match with grade movement. Florida 2008 grade 2 SC.2.P.8.6 asks students to measure and compare liquid volumes in differently shaped/sized containers (sources/2008/florida-2008-science-standards.txt:1103); grade 3 SC.3.P.8.2 asks students to measure and compare mass and volume of solids and liquids (line 1294). Concept continuity does not establish borrowing.

@graph.text: Recognize that matter is made of atoms and use models to represent atoms.
@graph.crosswalkNote: Medium-confidence partial concept match with grade movement. Florida 2008 grade 5 SC.5.P.8.4 describes atomic theory and matter composed of parts too small to see (sources/2008/florida-2008-science-standards.txt:1788–1789), while grade 8 SC.8.P.8.7 addresses atomic structure and subatomic particles. The predecessor supports atom-based matter, not the full model/history package.

@graph.evidence: human-reviewed concept continuity; not a textual-source finding. Register note: High-confidence concept match for comparing Solar-System objects, with cross-grade and scope qualifications. Florida 2008 grade 5 SC.5.E.5.3 lists the Sun, planets, moons, asteroids, and comets and locates Earth in the system (sources/2008/florida-2008-science-standards.txt:1727–1728). Grade 8 SC.8.E.5.7 asks students to compare properties of Solar-System objects to Earth, including gravity, distance from the Sun, speed/movement, temperature, and atmosphere (lines 2469–2471). The grade-5 draft compares those object types, includes characteristics such as composition, atmosphere, temperature, rings, and moons, and uses observational data (sources/2026/fl-k5.txt:4679–4716). It does not state several specific Earth-relative comparisons from the grade-8 benchmark, including gravity and orbital speed/distance. The draft adds evidence and historical-change tasks. Conceptual continuity does not establish borrowing. @graph.text: Recognize that the Universe is expanding.
@graph.crosswalkNote: Divergence dimension: explicit cosmological content. The 2008 middle-school benchmarks name galaxies and the universe’s scale; the high-school benchmark asks for evidence for Big Bang theory. The 1996 high-school SC.B.2.4 connects universe structure with matter/energy and says all matter/energy ever existed; 1996 SC.E.2.2 and surviving GLE SC.E.2.2.1 discuss distant stars and universe vastness. None of these located benchmark statements explicitly names expansion. The 2026 grade-8 benchmark explicitly states that the universe is expanding, and its example models galaxies moving farther apart. This is a more explicit benchmark-level expansion claim; the 2008 Big Bang evidence task could permit related instruction, so this is not proof that expansion was absent from prior teaching or a unique drafting source.

@graph.text: Interpret pressure-volume diagrams to identify work and thermodynamic process types.
@graph.crosswalkNote: Divergence dimension: task specificity and graphical representation. Florida 2008 asks students to compare work and power and explain entropy’s role in energy-to-work efficiency; the 1996 high-school energy expectations connect the first law with work/heat transfer and state that usable energy decreases. The surviving 1998/99 grades 6–8 GLE says energy conversions are not 100% efficient, but it is not a high-school GLE and does not specify pressure–volume diagrams. The 2026 benchmark adds pressure–volume diagrams, the area-under-the-curve interpretation of work, and qualitative identification of isobaric, isochoric, isothermal, and adiabatic processes. Grade placement remains high school.

@graph.text: Standard 1: The student recognizes that energy may be changed in form with varying efficiency. (SC.B.1.4) 1. understands how knowledge of energy is funda- mental to all the scientific disciplines (e.g., the energy required for biological processes in living organisms and the energy required for the build- ing, erosion, and rebuilding of the Earth). 2. understands that there is conservation of mass and energy when matter is transformed. 3. knows that temperature is a measure of the aver- age translational kinetic energy of motion of the molecules in an object. 4. knows that as electrical charges oscillate, they cre- ate time-varying electric and magnetic fields that propagate away from the source as an electromag- netic wave. 5. knows that each source of energy presents advan- tages and disadvantages to its use in society (e.g., political and economic implications may deter- mine a society’s selection of renewable or nonre- newable energy sources). 6. knows that the first law of thermodynamics re- lates the transfer of energy to the work done and the heat transferred. 7. knows that the total amount of usable energy al- ways decreases, even though the total amount of energy is conserved in any transfer.

Second 1. understands that, through the use of science processes, people can solve problems and make decisions. 2. analyzes information to make predictions, makes sketches and diagrams to explain ideas, draws conclusions using information and prior knowledge. 3. keeps science records.
